item.title: The case for BCacheFS inclusion in PVE
item.author: invalid@example.com (alexskysilk)
item.dc:creator: alexskysilk
item.content:encoded:
PVE has (and continues to have) a large presence in the homelab/self hosting crowd. The Primary filesystem option employed for single host applications was and is ZFS, due to its robust featureset and code maturity. Yet ZFS's core structural geometry—fixed virtual device (vdev) layouts, rigid pool topologies, and bolt-on workarounds like RAIDZ expansion or special vdevs—shows strain when modern single-node servers mix NVMe, SATA SSDs, and high-capacity hard drives. item.title: After a ransomware hit, how do you check PBS snapshots for signs of compromise before restoring?
item.author: invalid@example.com (UriShay-CyberSnap)
item.dc:creator: UriShay-CyberSnap
item.content:encoded:
Question for people who've had to restore VMs after an incident. Verify jobs tell you the chunks are intact, but they don't tell you if the attacker was already inside the guest when the backup ran. How are you deciding how far back to go? Mounting old snapshots in an isolated VM and scanning, checking file changes between snapshots, something else? Curious what actually works at scale with dozens of VMs.

Disclosure: I'm the founder of CyberSnap, which does snapshot compromise checks.
